# Clinical Vignette: Linh

Linh sits in the waiting room with her shoulders drawn inward, fingers tracing the edge of her phone screen without actually looking at it. At forty-nine, she carries herself with the careful precision of someone who has learned to take up as little space as possible. Her dark hair is pulled back tightly, and she wears the kind of neutral clothing—gray cardigan, black pants—that seems designed not to be noticed.

She came to the United States when she was fourteen, part of the wave of Southeast Asian refugees in the 1980s. Her parents worked in a textile factory; she was bright and quiet, the kind of child teachers forgot was in the classroom. By her twenties, she had built a stable life—a decent job in IT support, a marriage that eventually didn't work out, an apartment in a modest neighborhood. She had constructed a version of normalcy so carefully that most people who knew her casually had no idea about the first fourteen years of her life.

The truth is that Linh spent much of her childhood in a war zone. Her memories before America are fragmented—she describes them as if looking through water, distorted and incomplete. She remembers the sound of helicopters, the way her mother would pull her and her siblings under a table. She remembers hunger. She remembers a soldier—she's not entirely sure which side—and a moment of violence she can't quite articulate. She was young enough that some of it feels dreamlike, but her body remembers in ways her mind cannot quite access.

For decades, she managed. Work was predictable. She answered calls from frustrated users, walked them through password resets and connectivity issues, documented problems in careful tickets. The routine was soothing. At home, she kept her apartment orderly, avoided crowds, didn't date much after the divorce. This wasn't living so much as it was a kind of sustained holding of breath.

Three years ago, something shifted. A coworker was joking around, making loud noises and pretending to shoot people with a pen. It was stupid office humor, completely benign. But Linh found herself on the floor before she understood what was happening—her body had simply decided it was under fire. Her heart wouldn't slow down for hours. She called in sick the next day, and the day after that.

Since then, the symptoms have accumulated like snow. She startles at sounds—car backfires send her into a state of high alert that takes hours to resolve. She's developed insomnia; her mind races at night, cycling through half-remembered images and a constant low-level sense of dread. Some nights she lies awake for hours, her body tense, waiting for something she cannot name. At work, she's become hypervigilant, noticing every sound, every movement in her peripheral vision. She's made mistakes because she can't concentrate. Her manager has noticed her performance declining.

The worst part is the intrusive thoughts. Sometimes, entirely unbidden, she's back in that moment—the one she can't quite remember but feels in her bones. Her chest tightens. She can't breathe properly. It passes, but it leaves her shaken for the rest of the day. She's started avoiding certain areas of the office where she feels trapped. She's avoided the grocery store on the street where there was a car accident last month.

She tells herself that she's fine, that this is manageable, that she's survived worse. But she's not fine. She's exhausted. She's lonely in a way that feels permanent. And she's beginning to wonder if this is simply what the rest of her life will feel like.
